intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains what the slide is for, how to remember it and where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, check yourself against the recall questions, and write your own notes in the margin next to mine.

sections.title: What Counts as Work
sections.big_idea: Work is wider than a paid job. What the statistics **leave uncounted**, mostly women's care, decides who is seen, valued and protected.
in_plain_words: The 2013 ICLS-19 definition names five forms of work: employment for pay or profit, own-use production, volunteer work, unpaid trainee work and other forms such as unpaid care. National accounts and most labour statistics measure only the first. The System of National Accounts then draws its own line, which puts subsistence farming inside GDP and unpaid domestic work outside it.

India's 2019 Time Use Survey shows what falls outside. Women aged 15 and over spent about 299 minutes a day on unpaid domestic services for their household, and men about 97. Layer the workforce into formal employment, informal wage work and self-employment, and about 90% of Indian workers turn out to be informal. Every later section builds on that picture.

diagram.caption: how work is organised in India, top layer first

key_terms.meaning: The 2013 statistical definition of work, with five forms.
The accounting line that decides which production enters GDP.
Goods or services made for the household's own use.
NSO survey of how people spend a day; first national round in 2019.
Looking after people and households, paid or unpaid.
Work without a written contract or full social security.

worked_example.title: Size the time-use gap
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's 2019 Time Use Survey figures: women spend 299 minutes a day on unpaid domestic services, men 97.
steps: Gap in minutes: 299 − 97 = 202.
Gap in hours: 202 ÷ 60 = 3.4.
Ratio of women's time to men's: 299 ÷ 97 = 3.1.
Read it plainly: for every hour a man spends, a woman spends about three.
worked_example.answer: A gap of 202 minutes, about 3.4 hours a day, with women doing roughly three times the unpaid domestic work.

mistakes: Treating work and paid employment as the same thing, which removes subsistence farming, household production and care from the picture.
Reading the GDP boundary as a verdict that unpaid care has no value. It is an accounting convention, and the convention has consequences.
Designing a labour programme around the formal 10% and assuming it reaches everyone else.
Choosing a unit of analysis (household, individual, enterprise, value chain) without asking whose work it leaves out.

recall.q: How many forms of work does ICLS-19 recognise?
recall.a: Five: employment, own-use production, volunteer, unpaid trainee and other forms including unpaid care.

recall.q: Is unpaid care for household members inside the SNA boundary?
recall.a: No. It is outside the SNA boundary but inside the general production boundary.

recall.q: What did the 2019 Time Use Survey find about unpaid domestic services?
recall.a: Women spent about 299 minutes a day and men about 97.

recall.q: Roughly what share of Indian workers are informal?
recall.a: About 90%.

recall.q: What is the first decision in a livelihoods or labour project?
recall.a: Whose work counts, which fixes the unit of analysis.

sections.title: The Sustainable Livelihoods Framework
sections.big_idea: A household holds a portfolio of five capitals, meets risk, and turns assets into outcomes. **Find the binding constraint** before you design.
in_plain_words: The framework came from Chambers and Conway in 1991 and was refined by Scoones in 1998. It starts with how a household makes a living overall, with several income sources, and treats risk as an everyday condition. The five capitals are human, natural, physical, financial and social, and later writers added political capital.

Read the standard diagram left to right and then back again. Shocks, trends and seasonality shape what a household has. Institutions and policies decide access. Strategies such as intensification, diversification and migration produce outcomes, which feed the next round of assets. **Its critics point to power, class, gender and caste**, so use it as one lens among several.

diagram.caption: the DFID framework, with outcomes feeding back into assets

key_terms.meaning: An asset stock a household draws on: human, natural, physical, financial or social.
Shocks, trends and seasonality over which a household has little control.
How assets are deployed: intensification, diversification or migration.
Spreading risk across several income sources, farm and non-farm.
A sixth capital some authors add: voice and the ability to shape rules.

worked_example.title: Sort a household's assets into capitals
worked_example.setup: An illustrative village household lists what it has. Place each item under its capital.
steps: Two hectares of rain-fed land and a share of the village pond: natural capital.
A bullock cart and a hand pump: physical capital.
Savings of a few thousand rupees and an SHG loan line: financial capital.
A daughter with a vocational certificate and a father in good health: human capital.
Membership of the SHG and kin in the next town: social capital.
worked_example.answer: Natural, physical, financial, human and social. Ask next which capital is shortest, because that is the likely binding constraint.

mistakes: Addressing one capital (more credit, more training, more land) when the binding constraint sits in another.
Treating vulnerability as an emergency category when seasonality and shocks are normal conditions.
Applying the household as one unit and missing inequality inside it, especially by gender.
Calling an intervention a success when it runs down natural or social capital.

recall.q: Who gave the field its working definition of a livelihood, and when?
recall.a: Robert Chambers and Gordon Conway, in 1991.

recall.q: Name the five capitals.
recall.a: Human, natural, physical, financial and social.

recall.q: What are the three broad strategies in Scoones 1998?
recall.a: Agricultural intensification or extensification, livelihood diversification and migration.

recall.q: Give two critiques of the framework.
recall.a: It depoliticises, and it hides class, gender and caste inside the household.

recall.q: What does the framework ask of an evaluator?
recall.a: Whether outcomes improved without the asset base being depleted.

sections.title: Rural Livelihoods in India
sections.big_idea: Rural households **stitch together** farming, wages, commons, migration and group schemes. Programmes built on a single sector miss that portfolio.
in_plain_words: About 46% of the workforce is in agriculture and allied sectors, yet agriculture is about 18% of GVA, and 86% of holdings are under 2 hectares. Debt, input costs, climate stress and weak market access make up the agrarian distress list. MGNREGA gives a wage floor, with a note that the Act was repealed from 1 July 2026 and replaced by a 125-day guarantee.

Beyond the farm sit the commons and forest produce, which supply 15 to 25% of income in rain-fed semi-arid villages, circular migration, a growing non-farm economy, and aggregation through SHGs, FPOs and cooperatives. **Workers move, while entitlements stay anchored at home**, which is why portable protection is the binding policy challenge.

key_terms.meaning: The 2005 Act guaranteeing 100 days of rural wage work; the deck notes its 2026 replacement.
Non-timber forest products such as mahua, tendu leaves, lac and honey.
Repeated short-term moves for work, usually seasonal.
Self-help group: a savings and credit group, mostly of women.
Farmer producer organisation that aggregates small farmers' market power.
Moving into non-farm work because farm returns are too low.

worked_example.title: What does the average farm household owe?
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's figures: average agricultural household monthly income about ₹10,218, with about half from cultivation, and average outstanding debt ₹74,121.
steps: Cultivation income: 10,218 ÷ 2 = 5,109 rupees a month.
The other half comes from wages, livestock and non-farm work: 10,218 − 5,109 = 5,109.
Debt measured in months of income: 74,121 ÷ 10,218 = 7.3.
Read it plainly: the average debt equals about seven months of total household income.
worked_example.answer: About ₹5,109 a month from cultivation and the same from other sources, with debt worth about 7.3 months of income.

mistakes: Treating rural India as a synonym for agriculture when non-farm work is about 45% of the rural workforce.
Quoting MGNREGA's 100-day guarantee as current law without checking the 2026 replacement.
Reading all non-farm work as dynamic when much of it is distress-driven casual labour.
Assuming SHGs raise livelihood incomes because they raise savings and mobility.

recall.q: What share of operational holdings is under 2 hectares?
recall.a: 86%, per the Agriculture Census 2015-16.

recall.q: What share of household income did Jodha find from commons in rain-fed semi-arid villages?
recall.a: 15 to 25%, and 30% or more for the poorest.

recall.q: How many internal migrants did the 2011 Census count, and how many moved mainly for work?
recall.a: About 450 million, of whom about 46 million moved primarily for work.

recall.q: Which four legs does the policy slide say must work together?
recall.a: Non-farm employment, the MGNREGA wage floor, labour-mobility infrastructure and portable social protection.

recall.q: What is the unit of design in rural India?
recall.a: The household, over several years, with a diversified portfolio.

sections.title: The Indian Labour Market: A Map
sections.big_idea: Three ratios describe the labour market. **Low unemployment with low participation** means people have stopped looking, which is not good news.
in_plain_words: LFPR counts the employed and the unemployed seeking work against the working-age population. WPR counts the employed alone against that population. The unemployment rate divides the unemployed by the labour force. PLFS 2022-23 gives LFPR of about 57.9%, WPR about 56.0%, unemployment about 3.2% and female LFPR about 37% against about 78% for men.

Female participation fell from about 33% to about 23% before recovering, and the deck lists six explanations that interact: income effects, care burden, norms, demand, education and measurement. The workforce is also cut four ways (organised, formal, wage, public). **About 90% are informal**, and structural change went from agriculture to construction and informal services.

diagram.note: WPR uses employed only; UR divides unemployed by the labour force

key_terms.meaning: Labour force participation rate: employed plus seeking work, over working-age population.
Worker population ratio: employed over working-age population.
Unemployed and seeking work, as a share of the labour force.
Status over 365 days, principal plus subsidiary.
Status in the seven days before the survey.
Manufacturing stuck at 11 to 14% of workers for two decades.

worked_example.title: Three ratios from one population
worked_example.setup: An illustrative district has 1,000 working-age people: 560 employed, 18 unemployed and seeking work, and the rest outside the labour force.
steps: Labour force: 560 + 18 = 578.
Unemployment rate: 18 ÷ 578 = 3.1%.
People outside the labour force: 1,000 − 578 = 422, who are in no figure for unemployment.
worked_example.answer: LFPR 57.8%, WPR 56.0%, unemployment 3.1%, with 422 people outside the labour force.

mistakes: Quoting the unemployment rate without LFPR, which hides people who are not seeking work.
Mixing PLFS and CMIE figures without naming the source and method.
Comparing female LFPR across the 2017-18 series break as if it were one series.
Equating organised with formal, though one describes the enterprise and the other the worker.

recall.q: What is the formula for the unemployment rate?
recall.a: Unemployed divided by the labour force.

recall.q: What were the PLFS 2022-23 LFPR and unemployment rate?
recall.a: About 57.9% and about 3.2%.

recall.q: Name three of the six explanations for low female participation.
recall.a: Any three of: income effect, care burden, norms, demand side, education paradox, measurement.

recall.q: What was the share of agriculture in 2022-23?
recall.a: About 46%.

recall.q: What should you default-assume when you meet a worker?
recall.a: Informality: no written contract, no social security and irregular wages.

sections.title: Informal Work, Where Most Indians Are
sections.big_idea: Informal describes **missing protection**, and it describes most Indian work. Design for the whole 90% as well as the 10%.
in_plain_words: The ILO and NCEUS define informal employment as work without legal protection, social security or a written contract. NCEUS put the share at 92% in 2007, and the deck says it now sits at 85 to 90%. Informal does not mean illegal. Three groups fall within it: informal wage workers, the informal self-employed and casual wage workers.

The section then reads like a casebook. SEWA joined union and cooperative functions. Street vendors won the 2014 Act and still wait for committees. Domestic workers are visible but excluded from the 2019 to 2020 codes. Construction workers have a strong law and a large cess fund that is **mostly unspent**. Implementation is the common weak point.

children.label: Informal wage workers
items: No written contract or social security

diagram.caption: the three groups inside informal employment

key_terms.meaning: National Commission for Enterprises in the Unorganised Sector, chaired by Arjun Sengupta.
Breman's term for mobile workers with no secure employer.
Town Vending Committee, the municipal body under the 2014 street vendors law.
A 1% levy on construction project costs paid into state welfare boards.
The ILO Domestic Workers Convention of 2011, which India has not ratified.

worked_example.title: Informal and formal in crores
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's rough figures: a workforce of about 57 crore, of whom about 90% are informal.
steps: Informal workers: 57 × 0.9 = 51.3 crore.
Formal workers: 57 − 51.3 = 5.7 crore.
Compare with construction, the largest non-farm employer, at about 70 million workers, which is 7 crore.
Read it plainly: formal workers number fewer than the construction workers alone.
worked_example.answer: About 51.3 crore informal and 5.7 crore formal workers, so the formal group is smaller than the 7 crore in construction alone.

mistakes: Using informal as a synonym for illegal. Most informal work is legal and sits outside the protective frame.
Judging a law by its text. The BOCW Act is well designed and still under-delivers because boards disburse little.
Assuming street vendors are protected because a good Act exists, when many cities have no functional TVC.
Overlooking domestic workers because they are largely excluded from the 2019 to 2020 codes.

recall.q: What share of the workforce did NCEUS put in informal employment in 2007?
Who founded SEWA, and when?
recall.a: Ela Bhatt, in Ahmedabad in 1972.

recall.q: Which Act protects street vendors and when was it passed?
recall.a: The Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act, 2014.

recall.q: What is the cess rate for construction welfare?
recall.a: 1% on construction project costs.

recall.q: Which ILO conventions has India not ratified on domestic work and workplace violence?
recall.a: Convention 189 and Convention 190.

sections.title: Wages, Inequality & Penalties
sections.big_idea: A wage is a price and a social contract. **Minimum, needs-based and living wages** are three different benchmarks, so name the one you mean.
in_plain_words: Wages are set by minimum-wage notifications, bonus law, wage boards, pay commissions, bargaining and, for most informal workers, the market. Studies on the slide find that 25 to 50% of informal wage workers earn below the notified minimum. Casual men earn about ₹400 a day and women about ₹280, a raw gap near 30%.

Controls do not remove the gap. Decompositions attribute 30 to 50% of it to the unexplained part, and SC and ST workers earn 15 to 20% less than upper-caste workers with similar measured characteristics. At the top, **the top 1% hold about 22.6% of income** and about 40% of wealth, so wage policy has to sit beside tax policy.

left.title: Minimum wage
items: Below it for 25 to 50% of informal workers

right.title: Living wage
items: Meets needs of worker and dependants
Includes a small margin for shocks

key_terms.meaning: A notified legal floor, set by sector and region.
Enough for basic needs of a worker and dependants plus a small margin.
A gender gap that is widest at the bottom of the distribution.
A gap that also widens at the top because few women reach senior posts.
A decomposition splitting a gap into explained and unexplained parts.
The portion of national income paid as wages; it has fallen as profit share rose.

worked_example.title: The raw wage gap and its unexplained share
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's casual daily wages: ₹400 for men and ₹280 for women, and the finding that 30 to 50% of a gap is unexplained.
steps: Gap in rupees: 400 − 280 = 120.
Gap as a share of the male wage: 120 ÷ 400 = 30%.
Low end of the unexplained part: 30 × 0.3 = 9 percentage points.
High end of the unexplained part: 30 × 0.5 = 15 percentage points.
worked_example.answer: A 30% raw gap, of which 9 to 15 percentage points would be unexplained by measured characteristics.

mistakes: Treating the notified minimum wage as what workers receive. Compliance is lowest in agriculture, construction and domestic work.
Assuming controls for education and occupation explain the gender or caste gap away.
Using minimum wage, the 15th ILC formula and a living wage as if they were one benchmark.
Reading an inequality figure as a wage figure. Top incomes are mostly capital income.

recall.q: What national minimum wage did the Satpathy Committee recommend?
recall.a: ₹375 a day.

recall.q: What is the SC and ST wage penalty?
recall.a: 15 to 20% less than upper-caste workers with similar measured characteristics.

recall.q: Name the three mechanisms behind the caste penalty.
recall.a: Direct wage discrimination, occupational sorting and network exclusion.

recall.q: What did Reptakos Brett add to the 15th ILC needs-based formula?
recall.a: A 25% provision for education, medical needs, recreation and social obligations.

recall.q: What share of national income goes to the top 1%?
recall.a: About 22.6% in 2022-23, per WIL estimates.

sections.title: Labour Law & the 2019-20 Codes
sections.big_idea: Twenty-nine laws became **four Codes**. The text changes thresholds and definitions, and enforcement decides whether any of it reaches a worker.
in_plain_words: The Constitution frames labour as a state duty: Articles 23 and 24 are fundamental rights, while Articles 39 to 43A guide policy. The Supreme Court has used them to read fundamental rights widely, in cases such as Olga Tellis and Bandhua Mukti Morcha. Before 2019 the law sat in 29 or more central statutes.

The Codes cover wages (2019), industrial relations, safety and working conditions, and social security (all 2020). All four came into force on 21 November 2025 and central rules followed on 8 May 2026, while state rules are still being notified. Watch the thresholds: the **permission threshold moved from 100 to 300 workers**. The deck's verdict is that the jury is still out.

diagram.caption: what each Code replaces and one thing it changes

key_terms.meaning: Constitutional guides to state policy that courts do not enforce directly.
A national minimum below which states cannot set their own.
Establishment size above which prior government permission is needed.
Formalised by the IR Code, with benefit parity and no job security.
Mandatory under the OSH Code; aimed at a driver of informality.
1 to 2% of turnover, capped at 5% of gig worker payments.

worked_example.title: Apply the thresholds
worked_example.setup: An illustrative factory employs 250 workers and wants to lay off staff. Check old and new rules using the deck's thresholds.
steps: Old threshold for prior permission was 100 workers. Since 250 is above 100, permission was needed.
New threshold under the IR Code is 300 workers. Since 250 is below 300, permission is no longer needed.
Working week under the OSH Code: 48 ÷ 8 = 6 standard days.
Overtime cap per month, spreading 125 hours over a quarter: 125 ÷ 3 = 41.7 hours.
worked_example.answer: The factory needed permission before and does not now. A standard week is 6 days of 8 hours, with overtime capped near 41.7 hours a month on average.

mistakes: Citing pre-Code Acts as the law in force without checking the November 2025 commencement.
Assuming central rules are the whole picture when state rules are still being notified.
Setting aside old case-law. The deck says many concepts carry forward with modified contours.
Treating the floor wage as protection when it is set below most state minimums.

recall.q: Which Articles are fundamental rights on labour?
recall.a: Article 23 (forced labour) and Article 24 (child labour under 14).

recall.q: When did all four Codes come into force?
recall.a: 21 November 2025.

recall.q: How did the retrenchment permission threshold change?
recall.a: From 100 to 300 workers.

recall.q: What is the strike notice rule under the IR Code?
recall.a: Notice is mandatory in all industrial establishments, with no strike within 14 days of giving it.

recall.q: What new category does the Social Security Code recognise?
recall.a: Gig and platform workers, for the first time.

sections.title: Social Protection & Worker Welfare
sections.big_idea: India has built the frame of social protection. **Coverage and adequacy** for informal workers remain the unfinished work.
in_plain_words: Social protection covers contributory schemes such as EPF and ESI, tax-funded schemes such as PDS, MGNREGA, PM-KISAN and pensions, welfare boards and in-kind transfers. The ILO sets five domains across the life cycle. The coverage gap is largest for working-age protection: unemployment cover and maternity benefit for informal workers.

EPFO covers about 12% of the workforce, roughly 7 crore of 57 crore and ESIC reach is geographically limited. e-Shram has more than 30 crore registrations, but benefits beyond accident cover are slow to link. Tamil Nadu's welfare boards are the working model. **Map existing entitlements first**: the best intervention is often helping eligible workers claim what they already have.

left.title: Contributory
items: Reaches a small share of the workforce

key_terms.meaning: ILO Recommendation 202: a basic level of protection guaranteed to all.
Employees' Provident Fund Organisation, for establishments with 20 or more employees.
Employees' State Insurance, for workers earning up to ₹21,000 a month.
Central database of unorganised workers, launched in August 2021.
A body financed by cess or grants that gives benefits to a worker category.
National pension scheme for old age, widows and disability among BPL households.

worked_example.title: A month of EPF contributions
worked_example.setup: An illustrative worker has a wage base of ₹15,000 a month. Use the deck's rates: 12% each from worker and employer, with the employer share split 3.67% to EPF and 8.33% to EPS.
steps: Worker contribution: 15,000 × 0.12 = 1,800.
Employer contribution: 15,000 × 0.12 = 1,800.
Employer share to EPF: 15,000 × 0.0367 = 550.5.
Employer share to EPS pension: 15,000 × 0.0833 = 1,249.5.
worked_example.answer: ₹1,800 from the worker and ₹1,800 from the employer, of which ₹550.5 goes to EPF and ₹1,249.5 to the pension scheme.

mistakes: Counting a scheme as coverage because it exists. NSAP pensions of ₹200 to 500 a month from the centre are historically inadequate.
Assuming a registered e-Shram worker receives benefits beyond accident insurance.
Designing a new scheme before checking existing state welfare boards and entitlements.
Ignoring that health costs push about 5 crore Indians into poverty each year, and that out-of-pocket spending is above 50%.

recall.q: What are the four types of measure in the conceptual frame?
recall.a: Contributory schemes, tax-funded schemes, welfare boards and in-kind transfers.

recall.q: What is the EPF contribution rate?
recall.a: 12% from the employee and 12% from the employer.

recall.q: When was e-Shram launched and what is the free insurance cover?
recall.a: August 2021, with accident insurance up to ₹2 lakh under PMSBY.

recall.q: Which state model does the deck hold up for welfare boards?
recall.a: Tamil Nadu's, covering 38 or more scheduled employments.

recall.q: Where is India's coverage gap largest?
recall.a: Working-age protection, such as unemployment insurance and maternity benefit for informal workers.

sections.title: Gig, Platform & Future of Work
sections.big_idea: Platforms manage by **algorithm**, and the state laws so far create funds and registers. Wages, hours and algorithms remain open.
in_plain_words: The Social Security Code recognises gig and platform workers as a third category beside employees. NITI Aayog counted about 7.7 million gig workers in 2020-21 and projects about 23.5 million by 2029-30. Rajasthan in 2023 and Karnataka in 2025 passed state laws that fund welfare through a cess on aggregator turnover and require registration.

Algorithmic management controls allocation, pricing, performance and discipline, and workers see only their own data. Beyond platforms, the deck covers AI exposure, the care economy, which could add about 24 million jobs on a 2% of GDP investment, and a skilling system whose placement rates were around 25 to 30%. **Skilling alone has limited effect** without jobs and wage protection.

key_terms.meaning: SS Code 2020: earns from work outside a traditional employer-employee relationship.
A gig worker who gets work through an online platform.
The platform company that matches workers and customers.
Control of work by software that allocates, prices, rates and disciplines.
Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana, the flagship short-term skilling scheme.
Paid and unpaid work looking after children, elders and the sick.

worked_example.title: How big is the aggregator contribution?
worked_example.setup: An illustrative aggregator has annual turnover of ₹100 crore and pays ₹30 crore to gig workers. Use the SS Code rule: 1 to 2% of turnover, capped at 5% of payments to gig workers (reading the cap as a ceiling).
steps: At 1% of turnover: 100 × 0.01 = 1 crore.
At 2% of turnover: 100 × 0.02 = 2 crore.
Cap at 5% of payments: 30 × 0.05 = 1.5 crore.
The 2% rate would exceed the cap, so the contribution is held at 1.5 crore.
worked_example.answer: Between ₹1 crore and ₹1.5 crore, because the 5% cap on payments binds before 2% of turnover is reached.

mistakes: Calling gig workers employees. India's Code and the state laws treat them as a third category.
Assuming the Rajasthan or Karnataka laws give minimum wage or hour limits. They do not.
Treating a funded cess as a delivered benefit while the rules and fund operation are pending.
Reading AI exposure as job loss. The deck says displacement against augmentation is empirically open.

recall.q: How many gig workers did NITI Aayog count in 2020-21?
recall.a: About 7.7 million.

recall.q: Which was the first state law dedicated to gig workers?
recall.a: The Rajasthan Platform-based Gig Workers (Registration and Welfare) Act, 2023.

recall.q: Name two worker concerns about algorithmic management.
recall.a: Any two of: earnings below minimum wage, long hours, deactivation without process, unilateral pay changes, heat stress, no leave.

recall.q: What did evaluations find for PMKVY placements?
recall.a: Placement rates around 25 to 30%, mostly in low-wage informal roles.

recall.q: How many jobs could 2% of GDP in care create, according to the ILO?
recall.a: About 24 million, predominantly female.

sections.title: Trade Unions & Worker Organising
sections.big_idea: Wages follow **bargaining power**. Unions built for the mill struggle to reach contract, platform and informal work, and new forms are growing.
in_plain_words: Indian unions began in colonial mills and workshops: the Bombay Mill-Hands Association in 1884, the Madras Labour Union in 1918, AITUC in 1920 and the Trade Unions Act in 1926. Five federations, linked to parties, still dominate. Their claims differ from verified numbers, because the last official verification was in 2013.

Newer bodies organise domestic workers, hawkers, construction labour, app-based drivers and gig workers, while rural groups use MGNREGA, RTI and social audits. Recorded strikes have fallen sharply, but the deck says that is not industrial peace, since **disputes now occur in unrecognised workplaces**. Ambedkar's argument ties wages to the strength of organisation.

key_terms.meaning: Central trade union organisation recognised for national consultation.
Self Employed Women's Association, a union of self-employed women.
Sole bargaining agent where one union has 51% membership or more.
Public verification of works and payments, used as an organising tool.
An employer closure of a workplace, now more common than strikes.
Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan, the Rajasthan group behind RTI and right to work.

worked_example.title: Who is the negotiating union?
worked_example.setup: An illustrative plant has 400 workers. Under the IR Code, a single negotiating union exists if any union has 51% or more of members; otherwise there is a negotiating council. Union A has 210 members, union B has 150.
steps: Union A's share: 210 ÷ 400 = 52.5%.
Union B's share: 150 ÷ 400 = 37.5%.
Union A is above 51%, so it is the single negotiating union.
If A had 190 members, 190 ÷ 400 = 47.5% would fall short, and a council would be formed.
worked_example.answer: Union A, at 52.5%, is the single negotiating union.

mistakes: Using claimed membership as if it were verified. The last verification was in 2013.
Reading falling strike counts as industrial peace when disputes move to unrecorded workplaces.
Assuming unions and cooperatives are separate forms. SEWA combined them.
Overlooking rural labour organising, where entitlements such as MGNREGA became a platform.

recall.q: Which union is widely cited as India's first registered trade union?
recall.a: The Madras Labour Union of 1918, under B.P. Wadia.

recall.q: When was AITUC founded and who was its first president?
recall.a: 1920, with Lala Lajpat Rai as first president.

recall.q: What did SEWA change conceptually?
recall.a: It showed the self-employed can be organised as workers, combining union and cooperative functions.

recall.q: Which general strike against the four labour codes is the most recent on the slide?
recall.a: 12 February 2026.

recall.q: Which scholar's labour policy frames the closing argument?
recall.a: B.R. Ambedkar's, as Labour Member of the Viceroy's Executive Council from 1942 to 1946.

sections.title: Climate, Migration & Work in Transition
sections.big_idea: Heat, movement, structural change, fossil-fuel exit and AI all land on workers. **Decent work** is the measure, and India's growth has fallen short of it.
in_plain_words: The ILO projects about 5.8% of working hours lost in India by 2030 to heat stress, mostly in agriculture and construction. India has no statutory heat threshold for outdoor work. Migration is the main form of diversification for poor households: the 2011 Census counted about 454 million migrants and short-term circular migrants number 60 to 100 million.

Workers leave agriculture for construction and low-end services, while modern manufacturing stays small. A just transition for about 3 million coal-dependent workers needs income support, reskilling and attention to contract workers. Care work and AI exposure are the other pressures. The ILO decent work agenda has **four pillars**, and the closing frame says there is no development without decent work.

key_terms.meaning: A city or state plan for heat events; Ahmedabad's in 2013 was the first.
The 2020 return of migrant workers to home states.
A planned shift that protects workers from bearing the costs.
ILO 1999: productive work in freedom, equity, security and dignity.
Employment creation, rights at work, social protection and social dialogue.
India's tripartite programme, current cycle 2023 to 2027.

worked_example.title: What heat takes from a week's work
worked_example.setup: Apply the ILO's India-wide 5.8% loss to one illustrative worker: 48 hours a week, paid ₹400 for an 8-hour day (the deck's casual wage for men).
steps: Hours lost in a week: 48 × 0.058 = 2.8.
Hourly pay: 400 ÷ 8 = 50 rupees.
Pay lost in a week: 2.8 × 50 = 140 rupees.
This treats a national average as one worker's loss, so it only shows the order of magnitude.
worked_example.answer: About 2.8 hours and ₹140 a week in this illustration, the kind of income loss a heat policy should address.

mistakes: Treating heat as a health issue only when it is also an income and hours issue for informal workers.
Counting only Census migrants, which misses short-duration and circular movement.
Expecting workers leaving farms to enter jobs with social security. The slide says they mostly do not.
Taking any single estimate of AI exposure as settled when the evidence is open in 2026.

recall.q: What share of working hours does the ILO project lost to heat in India by 2030?
recall.a: About 5.8%.

recall.q: Which conventions has India not ratified among the ILO fundamental ones?
recall.a: Freedom of association and collective bargaining (87 and 98) and occupational safety and health (155 and 187).

recall.q: How many people depend directly and indirectly on India's coal economy?
recall.a: About 3 million workers.

recall.q: Which SDG targets does the deck link to decent work?
recall.a: SDG 8, with 5.4 on unpaid care, 1.3 on social protection and 10.4 on equality.

recall.q: When and where did Indian May Day observance begin?
recall.a: On 1 May 1923 in Madras, under M. Singaravelu Chettiar.

sections.title: Further Reading & Resources
sections.big_idea: Check the **definition and reference period** before comparing any two labour numbers. Different sources give systematically different answers.
in_plain_words: Official sources include PLFS, the older NSSO rounds, the Census, the Time Use Survey, ASI, the Labour Bureau, EPFO and e-Shram. Independent and international sources include CMIE, State of Working India, ILO reports, ILOSTAT, WIEGO, IHDS and the India Working Survey. The deck warns that reference periods differ across them.

The two reading lists give you classics on livelihoods (Chambers, Scoones, Ellis, Sen) and on Indian labour (Breman, Harriss-White, Ghosh, Kabeer), plus international theory from Lewis to Standing. The glossary is a quick reference. The charts show agriculture falling to 46%, a **labour share down from about 60% to 50%**, and female participation recovering mostly through family farm work.

key_terms.meaning: Periodic Labour Force Survey, annual since 2017-18.
Private monthly household survey with its own unemployment estimates.
State of Working India reports from Azim Premji University.
The span a survey asks about: 365 days, a week or a day.
Compensation of employees as a share of GVA.
A pointer to another ImpactMojo deck on a connected topic.

worked_example.title: How much did labour's share fall?
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's chart reading: labour share about 60% in the 1980s and about 50% by 2022.
steps: Fall in percentage points: 60 − 50 = 10.
Latest share as a fraction of the earlier one: 50 ÷ 60 = 83.3%.
Relative fall: 10 ÷ 60 = 16.7%.
Total wages can still rise if GVA grows, so share and level are different measures.
worked_example.answer: A fall of 10 percentage points, about one-sixth of labour's earlier slice.

mistakes: Comparing LFPR or unemployment across sources without checking the reference period.
Mixing the all-ages female LFPR chart (17.5% to 27.8%) with the age 15+ figures (23% to 37%).
Reading a falling labour share as falling wages. Total wages can rise while the share falls.
Using a reading list as a substitute for the primary data it points to.

recall.q: Which survey is the official annual source for labour force data?
recall.a: PLFS, run by MoSPI, annual since 2017-18.

recall.q: What is the difference between usual status and current weekly status?
recall.a: Usual status covers 365 days; current weekly status covers the seven days before the survey.

recall.q: Which classic paper is the dual-economy foundation in the labour reading list?
recall.a: W. Arthur Lewis, 'Economic Development with Unlimited Supplies of Labour' (1954).

recall.q: What does the chart on slide 98 show about construction?
recall.a: It grew from 2% to 13% of the workforce, absorbing the largest share of released labour.

recall.q: Which ImpactMojo decks does the cross-reference slide name?
recall.a: Development Economics 101, Politics of Aspiration 101, MEL Basics 101, Caste Studies 101, Inequality Basics 101 and Public Health 101.

notes.2: Twelve sections run from definitions to law, welfare, gig work and climate. Sections 1 to 3 give vocabulary and the rural base, 4 to 6 the numbers, 7 and 8 the rules, 9 to 11 the pressures on work. **Read in order the first time**, then use the agenda to jump back.
notes.4: Pick one example of each form from your own street: a shopkeeper, a farmer feeding her family, a volunteer, an intern, a daughter caring for a parent. The definition calls all five work, yet **only employment work enters national income accounts** and most labour statistics.
notes.5: The SNA boundary is an accounting convention, so ask who gains from where it sits. Women's 299 minutes a day of unpaid domestic services, against men's 97, falls **outside GDP and outside employment figures**. Inside means counted. Outside means invisible to policy.
notes.6: Think of care as the first shift that makes every other shift possible. The slide gives two sizes for it: about 9% of global GDP at minimum wage, and 7.5 to 15.4% of India's GDP depending on method. **The range itself teaches you** that the answer depends on how you value an hour.
notes.7: Draw three layers and write the share beside each: about 10% formal, roughly half of wage employment informal, 50 to 55% self-employed. The 90% figure comes from adding the bottom two layers. **Keep this as your default picture** of any Indian worker you meet.
notes.8: This slide gives two tests to run before any project. Whose work counts in your design? Which unit of analysis (household, individual, enterprise or value chain) are you using? **The unit you pick decides what you see.** The deck labels the quote as its summary of Ela Bhatt, so cite it that way.
notes.10: Hold the lineage in two names and two dates: Chambers and Conway in 1991, then Scoones in 1998 as the version most people cite. The six shifts on the slide all move attention **from output per acre to how a household makes a living** across several income sources.
notes.11: Trace the arrows with a finger, then trace the feedback. Vulnerability shapes assets, structures filter access to them, strategies turn assets into outcomes, and outcomes **restock the assets** for the next round. If your project skips a box, name which one and why.
notes.12: Learn the capitals as human, natural, physical, financial and social. For any household, ask which is shortest, because that is the likely constraint. **A project that adds more of an abundant capital will leave the outcome where it was.** Political capital is the later sixth.
notes.13: Treat risk as weather that returns every year. Shocks arrive suddenly, trends build over decades and seasonality repeats on a calendar. The slide's claim is that **lean-season distress migration** is largely driven by the agrarian calendar, so mark peak and lean months before designing year-round work.
notes.14: Households mix strategies. The slide's example is a small farm worked by elders, adult children migrating seasonally, plus NREGA wages and livestock. When you interview a household, **list every income source** and match each to a strategy. Outcomes cover income, food security, vulnerability and capability.
notes.15: Read the left column as questions to ask of any livelihoods study: who holds power, which class, which global links, which gender, which caste. The right column says what the framework still does well. **Use it as one lens among several**, with these gaps in mind.
notes.16: Run two tests on a proposal. First, which capital does it add, and is that the binding constraint? The evaluator's test comes second: **did outcomes improve without running down natural or social capital?** A project that passes the first and fails the second has borrowed from the future.
notes.18: Keep three numbers: about 46% of workers in agriculture, about 18% of GVA from it, and 86% of holdings under 2 hectares. Set the first two side by side, because **many workers share a small slice of output**. Check each figure's survey year before you quote it.
notes.19: Read the left column as a causal chain: small plots, rising costs, flat yields, debt, climate stress and weak market access. The suicide figures on the right are the visible end. **Quote the debt data** (50.2% of households indebted, ₹74,121 on average) when someone asks how deep distress runs.
notes.20: Note the slide's own flag: MGNREGA was repealed from 1 July 2026 and replaced by the Viksit Bharat G RAM G Act 2025, which raises the guarantee to 125 days. The evidence column describes the 100-day guarantee. **Check which Act a figure belongs to** before you cite it.
notes.21: Jodha's numbers give the weight: commons supply 15 to 25% of household income in rain-fed semi-arid villages and 30% or more for the poorest. That is why **encroachment hits the poorest hardest**. Pair this with the Forest Rights Act row, where implementation is uneven.
notes.22: Keep three figures apart: about 450 million migrants in the 2011 Census, of whom about 46 million moved mainly for work, and about 100 million circular migrants in 2017. The last line is the policy point: **workers move while entitlements stay at home**, so portability is the challenge.
notes.23: Ask of any non-farm job whether the worker was pushed or pulled. Non-farm share rose from about 25% to about 45%, yet manufacturing stayed near 8%. **Distress and productive diversification need different policies**: skills training suits the second, wage floors the first.
notes.24: Sort the institutions by purpose: SHGs for savings and women's mobility, FPOs for market power, cooperatives and producer companies as legal forms. The verdict is balanced: **SHGs help mobility and savings, with a mixed record on incomes**. None supplies market infrastructure or working capital.
notes.25: Compress the section into three design rules: design for the household, plan across years, diversify the portfolio. The policy paragraph names four legs: non-farm jobs, the MGNREGA wage floor, mobility infrastructure and portable social protection. **If one leg is missing, the structure wobbles.**
notes.27: Memorise three formulas. LFPR counts employed plus unemployed over working-age population, WPR counts only the employed, and UR divides the unemployed by the labour force. The denominators differ, which is the usual slip. Always **quote the source**, since PLFS and CMIE use different designs.
notes.28: Read the four numbers as a set. A 3.2% unemployment rate sits beside a 37% female LFPR, so a low unemployment rate says little about how many women are working. **People who are not seeking work are not counted as unemployed.** Look at LFPR first, then at youth and graduates.
notes.29: The chart tells a curve: down from about 33% in 2004-05 to about 23% in 2017-18, then back to about 37% by 2022-23. The slide warns that part of the recovery comes from measurement and women returning to family farms. **Note the series break in 2017-18** before comparing across it.
notes.30: Use the six explanations as a checklist, because they interact. Care burden has a number: 299 against 97 minutes a day. The GDP prize figures (18% and 27%) come from different studies, so **quote the order of magnitude** and leave the decimals aside.
notes.31: Keep the three cuts apart: organised against unorganised looks at the enterprise, formal against informal at the worker, wage against self-employment at the type of work. Internalise the closing figure: **about 90% of workers are informal**, even inside organised firms through contract labour.
notes.32: Sort sectors by share: agriculture about 46%, services about 28%, manufacturing and construction about 13% each. The story is the route taken, from agriculture to construction and informal services. **Manufacturing has sat at 11 to 14% for two decades**, which the slide calls the missing middle.
notes.33: This framing slide gives a default for fieldwork: assume informality until shown otherwise. That means no written contract, no security and irregular pay. The deck labels the quote as its own summary. **A programme built for formal workers helps the minority who need help least.**
notes.35: Remember that informal means unprotected, and that legal and informal go together. The three groups cover wage, self-employed and casual workers. NCEUS put the share at 92% in 2007, and the slide says it now sits at 85 to 90%. **Describe informality as a condition of work**, never as a crime.
notes.36: Take one idea from each scholar. Breman: decades of fieldwork on footloose labour in Gujarat. Harriss-White: informality as the structure of Indian capitalism. Her quotation claims it is **consolidating as the basic mode of work organisation**. Use the book lists as your reading order.
notes.37: SEWA is the model case of a hybrid form, a union and a cooperative in one body. Its services (bank, insurance, training, healthcare, child care) answer needs wage bargaining alone cannot. **Remember the founding facts: 1972, Ahmedabad, Ela Bhatt.** Section 10 returns to SEWA as a union.
notes.38: Treat the vendors' Act as the success story with a caveat. The 2014 law grants the right to vend, protection from eviction without process and seats on committees. The right column lists why the gap persists. **Where cities have no functional TVC, ask who is accountable.**
notes.39: Start with the legal gaps: India has ratified neither C189 nor C190, and the new codes exclude domestic workers. The slide counts about 4.1 million domestic workers from the 2011-12 NSS, which groups call an under-count. **Check state-level options before concluding nothing exists**, since some states have notified minimum wages and welfare boards.
notes.40: BOCW is the test of design against delivery. The 1% cess has built up a fund of more than ₹90,000 crore and only a fraction reaches workers. **The slide puts the failure down to governance** and calls the design sound. Ask what stops registration, especially for migrants.
notes.41: Take the three implications as design rules: protection follows the worker, collective forms combine union and cooperative functions, and regulation starts from informality and builds upward. **Write the rules on a card**, then test every proposal against them. The reading list is your starting shelf.
notes.43: List the six ways wages get set, then mark the one most informal workers face: market wages, often below the notified minimum. Studies on the slide find 25 to 50% of informal wage workers paid below it. **The minimum is a promise on paper for most workers.**
notes.44: Anchor on four numbers: about ₹20,000 monthly for regular workers, ₹25,000 in organised manufacturing, ₹400 a day for casual men and ₹280 for casual women. The raw gap of about 30% shows **before any controls**. In the trend list, note that casual real wages stagnated from 2014 to 2019.
notes.45: The raw gap is about 20% in regular work and 25 to 30% in casual work, and most of it survives controls. Sticky floor and glass ceiling name the two ends. **Decompositions put 30 to 50% of the gap in the unexplained part**, which the slide reads as discrimination.
notes.46: Memorise the 15 to 20% penalty and the three mechanisms: direct discrimination, occupational sorting and network exclusion. The penalty is smallest in public jobs, where rules are transparent. **Transparent rules shrink the gap**, which tells you where reform can start.
notes.47: Two figures carry the slide: the top 1% hold about 22.6% of income and about 40% of wealth. The trend list says the top share has roughly doubled since 1980 while the bottom 50% fell. **Top incomes are largely capital income**, so wage policy alone cannot reach them.
notes.48: Use the slide to ask which wage benchmark is on the table: statutory minimum, needs-based (15th ILC, 1957) or living wage. The needs-based formula adds 3 consumption units and 2,700 kcal, and Reptakos added 25%. The closing line says the choice **changes the policy ask**.
notes.49: This closing slide moves from description to demand: a living-wage floor, indexed to prices and enforced. It ranks this above most active labour-market programmes. The deck labels the quote as its summary. **Caste and gender penalties are structure**, so build them into design.
notes.51: Divide the table into two groups: fundamental rights (Articles 23 and 24) that courts enforce, and Directive Principles (39, 41, 42, 43, 43A) that steer state policy. The slide's point is that **courts have used the Directive Principles to read fundamental rights widely**, as in Olga Tellis.
notes.52: Treat the pre-Code list as the vocabulary of the case-law you will still read. Pair them: the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 for retrenchment and strikes, the Factories Act 1948 for safety. The six cases show **how courts widened 'industry' and the right to livelihood**.
notes.53: Read the table as old law on the left becoming new Code on the right. Wages absorbs four Acts, IR three, OSH many, Social Security the provident fund and insurance family. **All four Codes came into force on 21 November 2025**, with state rules pending. Check status before advising.
notes.54: Read the left column as the promise and the right as the doubts. A national floor wage set below most state minimums binds nobody. The definition of wages in Section 2(y) shapes PF, gratuity and bonus. **Run your own numbers on the wage base** before assuming costs.
notes.55: Focus on the 300-worker threshold: prior permission for retrenchment, layoff or closure rose from 100 to 300. Unions say that leaves roughly 75% of protected workers outside the rule, while industry says 100 was a brake on hiring. **The evidence on hiring is mixed**, so the dispute is political.
notes.56: Count what could help most: the mandatory appointment letter, aimed at a driver of informality. The trade-off line carries the warning, wider coverage with no matching rise in inspectors. **Coverage on paper helps only if someone inspects.** Note the 8-hour day and 48-hour week.
notes.57: Remember the firsts: statutory recognition of gig work, an aggregator contribution of 1 to 2% of turnover capped at 5% of payments, and e-Shram as the registration platform. The right column lists what is unfinished. **The national fund still has to start operating**, though states have begun.
notes.58: Hold the slide's verdict: the jury is still out. Two practical lessons follow. Lawyers read old case-law alongside the new Codes. Organisers answer the higher bar for collective action by **building density and combining union and cooperative work**. Check state rules for the details.
notes.60: Separate the four kinds of measures: contributory, tax-funded, welfare boards and in-kind. Then map them against the five life-cycle domains. The last paragraph tells you where India is weakest: **working-age protection**, meaning unemployment cover and maternity benefit for informal workers.
notes.61: Keep the percentages straight: EPF 12% from each side, with 3.67% to EPF and 8.33% to EPS; ESI 0.75% and 3.25%. The gap list explains why coverage is thin. **Splitting establishments to stay under the threshold is a known evasion route**, alongside contract labour.
notes.62: e-Shram is the registry: self-registration with Aadhaar and a bank account, with free accident cover up to ₹2 lakh. Its limits are in the right column. **A database delivers nothing until benefits attach to it.** Ask what a registered worker receives beyond accident insurance.
notes.63: Use Tamil Nadu as the working model: 38 or more scheduled employments, over 1 crore registered workers, a wide benefit list. The practitioner line is the action: **find the board for your worker category**, because the benefit may already exist. Awareness and registration are often the obstacle.
notes.64: Read the table as an inventory of what exists, then test adequacy. NSAP pensions of ₹200 to 500 a month from the centre, MGNREGA wages sometimes below the state minimum (the Act ran until 30 June 2026), weak PMAY coverage in urban informal settlements. The last sentence says **the frame is in place and the calibration remains the work**.
notes.65: Two numbers set the stakes: out-of-pocket spending above 50% of health spending, and about 5 crore pushed into poverty each year. The right column links occupations to hazards. **Match each worker group you serve to its hazard** on the list: silicosis, pesticides, heat, ergonomic injury.
notes.66: The unfinished agenda is a five-item list, so copy it out. The practitioner advice offers the quickest win: map existing entitlements first, because **helping eligible workers claim what they already hold often beats designing a new scheme**. The deck labels the framing as its own summary.
notes.68: Learn the two definitions as one idea: work and pay outside the employer-employee relationship, with platforms as intermediary. The key figure is NITI's 7.7 million in 2020-21 rising to 23.5 million. **India creates a third category**, while the UK, California, Spain and the EU each answer differently.
notes.69: Use the five control mechanisms as an audit checklist for any platform: allocation, pricing, performance, discipline and information asymmetry. The worker concerns list translates each into daily experience. **Ask what appeal a worker has before an account is deactivated.**
notes.70: Compare the two laws on one question: what do they create, and what do they leave out? Both create funding, registration and grievance handling. Neither gives employee status, minimum wage or hour limits, and both await rules. **Track Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Maharashtra** next.
notes.71: Remember the headline: 26% of Indian employment is in high-exposure occupations, against about 60% in the US. The exposed work sits in services such as BPO and support. **The net effect is open**, as the slide says, and depends on skilling and regulation.
notes.72: The care bet in numbers: 2% of GDP invested in care could generate about 24 million jobs, mostly for women. Public carers are about 14 lakh anganwadi workers and 10 lakh ASHAs. **The dignity question is pay**: they are called volunteers and receive honoraria.
notes.73: Skill India lists six institutions, and the evidence box is the point. PMKVY placement rates were around 25 to 30% with limited persistence, mostly in low-wage informal roles. **Skilling works best alongside jobs and wage protection.** Evaluators favour apprenticeship over classroom courses.
notes.74: Use the three forces as a lens on any labour-policy debate: platforms, AI and care. The three priorities are the actions: operationalise the gig fund, invest in care with fair pay, regulate algorithms. **The future of work is already the present** for gig and care workers.
notes.76: Read the timeline in two blocks: before 1920 (Bombay 1884, Madras 1918) and after (AITUC 1920, Trade Unions Act 1926, Meerut 1929, Industrial Disputes Act 1947). The closing box says unions built in mills and workshops have **struggled to follow work into small firms, contract labour and platforms**.
notes.77: Remember that the last verification was in 2013 and claimed membership diverges from verified counts. Learn the five federations and their lineages: CPI, Congress, socialist, RSS and CPI(M). **BMS usually stays out of joint platforms**; the most recent joint strike on the slide was 12 February 2026.
notes.78: SEWA changed who counts as a worker. Registered as a union in 1972, with about 2.5 million members and a cooperative bank from 1974, it argued the self-employed face the same problems as wage workers. **The vendor and the home-based producer are workers.** It shaped ILO Conventions 177 and 189.
notes.79: Use the left column as a directory by worker type and the right as the reasons organising is hard. The common thread is an employer that is hard to find, whether a chain of contractors or an algorithm. **Match each organisation to the difficulty it faces.**
notes.80: Rural labour is the hardest to organise, so look at the tools: MGNREGA entitlements, RTI petitions on muster rolls and social audits. The MKSS lineage shows one tradition produced both the right to information and the right to work. **An entitlement can become an organising platform.**
notes.81: Read the decline as a change in recording as much as in conflict. The right column gives reasons this is no peace: a smaller formal base, contract labour, closures replacing strikes and unrecorded disputes. **App-worker action is rising.** Name the flashpoints: Maruti Manesar, Toyota Bidadi, Wistron.
notes.82: The structural argument is short: wages follow bargaining power, and in a labour-surplus economy only collective bargaining gives a worker any. The deck labels the quote as its summary of Ambedkar's labour policy. **Skilling and enterprise programmes address one side** and leave voice untouched.
notes.84: The ILO projection is 5.8% of working hours lost in India by 2030, mostly in agriculture and construction. The policy-gap list names what is missing: no statutory heat threshold, a silent OSH Code, rare compensation. **Heat is an income problem for informal workers** as well as a health problem.
notes.85: Two estimates to reconcile: Census 2011 counts about 454 million migrants by last residence, while circular migrants number 60 to 100 million by various studies, because short moves slip past Census conventions. The right column lists post-2020 fixes and their gaps. **Remember SWAN and e-Shram.**
notes.86: Follow the share arrows: agriculture falls from about 60% to 42 to 45% of jobs, manufacturing stays near 12% and construction takes the leavers. The list explains the consequences, **including falling female participation** as women left farming faster than non-farm jobs opened.
notes.87: Just transition comes with a number (about 3 million coal-dependent workers) and a checklist of seven needs. Remember the coal districts and the fiscal stake, since states earn royalties. **Contract and informal workers are the majority in coal supply chains**, so plan for them.
notes.88: Two policy demands share one slide: recognise unpaid care as work and formalise paid carers. It counts about 2.4 million ASHAs and anganwadi workers on honoraria, matching slide 72, and about 4.1 million domestic workers. **Slide 39 gives the same NSS count**, so the two agree.
notes.89: Use the five open questions as a framework: distribution, speed, wage compression, skill obsolescence and bargaining. The exposure list puts white-collar and clerical work first and manual work lower in the short term. **Compare this slide with slide 71**, which cites the IMF's lower exposure for India; the ILO paper there finds middle-income countries less exposed too.
notes.90: Learn the four pillars of Decent Work: employment creation, rights at work, social protection and social dialogue. Then link them to SDG 8, 5.4, 1.3 and 10.4. **India has not ratified conventions 87 and 98**, and the slide calls that a policy choice, with domestic law covering most protections.
notes.91: This closing frame measures growth against decent work: incomes rose, but the share with secure jobs, contracts, security and a living wage did not keep pace. The May Day box gives the date: 1 May 1923 in Madras. **Link any theme you work on back to the conditions of work.**
notes.93: Sort sources by who produces them: official (PLFS, EUS, Census, TUS, ASI, Labour Bureau, EPFO, e-Shram) and independent or international. The data-quality note is the rule: reference periods differ and give systematically different LFPR and unemployment. **Check the definition before comparing numbers.**
notes.94: Use the list as a shelf with two halves: framework classics (Chambers, Scoones, Ellis, Sen) and Indian rural work (Drèze, Sainath, Breman, Khera). Start with Chambers and Conway 1991 and Scoones 1998. **Read Scoones 2009** when you want the critical retrospective.
notes.95: The list pairs Indian labour studies with international theory. Lewis 1954 is the foundational dual-economy paper. For informality read Breman and Harriss-White, and for women's work Ghosh, Kabeer and Mazumdar. **Pick one from each half** so you meet both the local and the global argument.
notes.96: Use the glossary as a quiz: cover the right column and define each term. Watch the reference periods, usual status over 365 days against weekly and daily. The table says the unorganised sector is **broader than informal**, so keep the two words apart. Five capitals appear here too.
notes.97: This second glossary is the legal toolkit. Learn each Code by its one-line job. The glossary says the Code on Wages is not yet fully operational in 2026, while slide 53 reports all four Codes in force. **Check current status before you cite either** statement in advice.
notes.98: Read the stacked areas from the top: agriculture falls from 68% to 46%, construction rises from 2% to 13%, manufacturing stays at 11 to 13%. The chart pictures slides 32 and 86. **Services growth sits in low-productivity informal activity**, which is the failed industrial transition.
notes.99: The Sankey follows about 57 crore workers from sector to formal or informal status. The caption says about 90% are informal, and many in the formal sector still lack contracts and benefits. **Formalisation has to happen inside each sector** as well as across sectors.
notes.100: Use the cards as a route map. Development Economics 101 gives the theory, Politics of Aspiration the rights framework, MEL Basics the design tools, and Caste Studies, Inequality Basics and Public Health the connected topics. **Pick the deck that matches your next task.**
notes.101: The closing quote states the organising thesis: workers win by acting together and lose alone. The two boxes say what the deck is for and where May Day began (Madras, 1923). **Finish by listing the four unfinished goals**: eight-hour day, living wage, social security, right to organise.
notes.102: The chart shows female LFPR for all ages: 17.5% in 2017-18 and 27.8% in 2022-23. Slide 29 uses age 15 and over and reads 23% and 37%, so **never mix the two series**. The slide adds that much of the rise is unpaid family work in agriculture.
notes.103: Labour's share of GVA fell from about 60% in the 1980s to about 50% by 2022. The final sentence is a useful warning: total wages can rise while the labour share falls. **Share and level are different measures.** Capital-intensive technology, weaker bargaining and informalisation are the listed causes.
